arXiv:2603.24787v1 [cs.AI] 25 Mar 2026

ReLope: KL-Regularized LoRA Probes for Multimodal LLM Routing

Yaopei Zeng Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University    Congchao Wang Affiliation: Amazon AGI    Blake JianHang Chen Affiliation: Google    Lu Lin Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University
Abstract

Routing has emerged as a promising strategy for balancing performance and cost in large language model (LLM) systems that combine lightweight models with powerful but expensive large models. Recent studies show that probe routing, which predicts the correctness of a small model using its hidden states, provides an effective solution in text-only LLMs. However, we observe that these probes degrade substantially when applied to multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). Through empirical analysis, we find that the presence of visual inputs weakens the separability of correctness signals in hidden states, making them harder to extract using standard probe designs. To address this challenge, we introduce two complementary approaches for improving probe routing in MLLMs. First, we propose the Attention Probe, which aggregates hidden states from the preceding layer based on attention scores to recover distributed correctness signals. Second, we present the KL-Regularized LoRA Probe (ReLope), which inserts a lightweight LoRA adapter and applies a KL regularizer to learn routing-aware representations. Comprehensive experiments show that our methods consistently outperform baselines, suggesting that improving the quality of hidden states is key to effective routing in MLLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/Spinozaaa/ReLope.

**footnotetext: Work done during the internship at Google. Correspondence to: Lu Lin <lulin@psu.edu>

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced and are now widely deployed in real-world applications (Zhao et al., 2023). However, their deployment faces a fundamental trade-off: large models provide strong performance but introduce substantial costs, while smaller models are cheaper but less capable. This tension has motivated the development of routing strategies, which dynamically decide whether a query can be handled by a lightweight model or should be escalated to a stronger one (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025; Jitkrittum et al., 2025). Such strategies enable hybrid LLM systems that achieve favorable trade-offs between performance and efficiency.

Most existing routing methods have been studied in the context of text-only LLMs. Recently, however, multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) (Yin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024) have emerged as a new foundation for AI systems capable of jointly processing text and visual inputs. While these models enable more complex reasoning tasks, they also introduce new challenges for efficient deployment. In particular, visual inputs significantly increase inference cost, creating an even stronger need for effective routing mechanisms in multimodal systems.

Among existing strategies, the trained probe has emerged as one of the most effective approaches Gupta et al. (2024); Chuang et al. (2025). It trains lightweight classifiers on hidden states of the small model to estimate whether the generated answer is correct. Compared with heuristic confidence measures such as token probabilities and average entropy (Huang et al., 2023; Mahaut et al., 2024), probes capture richer semantic signals from LLMs’ hidden states, leading to a strong ability in correctness estimation. Because probes operate directly on internal hidden states, they are also architecture-agnostic and, in principle, applicable across different model modalities. However, it remains unclear whether hidden state probes remain reliable when visual inputs are introduced. This naturally raises a research question: Can probe routings designed for text-only LLMs transfer effectively to MLLMs, and if not, how should they be adapted?

Through carefully designed experiments, we show that probes effective in text-only LLMs degrade in multimodal settings, achieving consistently lower AUC on queries containing images across multiple datasets. For example, when trained on ScienceQA (Saikh et al., 2022), probe performance drops substantially for questions containing images. This phenomenon is further confirmed on A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022) and MMMU (Yue et al., 2024). These results suggest that the hidden states produced by MLLMs provide weaker signals for predicting correctness.

To address this challenge, we propose two complementary techniques for improving probe routing in MLLMs. First, we introduce the Attention Probe, which aggregates token-level hidden states from the preceding layer using an attention mechanism. It recovers distributed correctness signals that may be diluted in the final token hidden state. Second, we propose the KL-Regularized LoRA Probe (ReLope), which adapts hidden representations through a lightweight Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) module (Hu et al., 2022) and regularizes them using a KL divergence inspired by the Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) theory (Alemi et al., 2016). This regularization encourages the model to learn compressed representations that retain information relevant for routing decisions while suppressing task-irrelevant visual noise. Comprehensive experiments show that both Attention Probe and ReLope consistently improve routing performance over existing baselines, with ReLope achieving the strongest trade-offs between accuracy and cost in hybrid MLLM systems.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We identify and empirically uncover a previously underexplored limitation of probe routing: its performance degrades in MLLMs due to weaker correctness signals in hidden states.

  • •

    We propose two effective routing techniques in MLLMs based on the trained probe: the Attention Probe, which aggregates token-level hidden states to recover distributed routing signals, and ReLope, which learns routing-aware representations via LoRA adaptation and KL regularization.

  • •

    Extensive experiments on five multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that our methods consistently outperform existing routing approaches, significantly improving routing quality while maintaining efficient inference in hybrid MLLM systems.

2 Related Work

2.1 Routing Before the Small Model

One family of methods determines routing decisions before querying the small model, relying only on the input queries (Shah and Shridhar, 2025; Ong et al., 2024; Panda et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Early works train a pretrained router to classify which model will succeed for a given query. Examples include classifier-based routers such as (Shnitzer et al., 2023) and SelectLLM (Ong et al., 2024), reward-based routers like (Lu et al., 2023), and cost-aware strategies like Routoo (Mohammadshahi et al., 2024). Others use non-pretrained strategies, such as Eagle (Zhao et al., 2024), which leverage heuristic selection without extra training.

These methods avoid invoking the small model when unnecessary, reducing cost. However, they are highly dependent on the quality of collected data for training or comparison. More importantly, these methods focus on the text-only prompts. When extending to MLLMs, their router architectures should be redesigned to incorporate additional modalities such as images or videos, which substantially increases implementation complexity.

2.2 Routing With the Small Model

A second class of methods leverages information from the small model. This includes both its final outputs (cascade) and hidden states probe. Cascade approaches run the small model and then apply a rule to decide whether escalation to the large model is needed according to the output of the small model. FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2023) highlights that cascades can substantially reduce cost while maintaining quality. Most subsequent strategies use different rules to evaluate the small model’s confidence as a routing score (Zhao et al., 2024; Chuang et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2023). For example, MoT Yue et al. (2023) applies multiple inferences and refers to the answer consistency to route. The work (Chuang et al., 2025) evaluates the performance of existing uncertainty estimation methods in the routing problem. Another work (Gupta et al., 2024) shows that sequence-level uncertainty is biased (favoring short or long generations), and proposes refined rules using token-level uncertainty quantiles.

Another line of work directly trains a probe on hidden states of the small model to predict whether its answer will be correct. Post-hoc embedding probe methods (Chuang et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2024; Mahaut et al., 2024) show that probes trained on intermediate layers can effectively capture correctness signals. These methods have achieved strong performance in text-only routing, balancing efficiency and reliability. However, we empirically observe that the introduction of images leads to degraded routing accuracy, motivating us to design new routing strategies.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Problem Definition.

We consider a hybrid MLLM system composed of a small model, such as an on-device model, and a large model that is more capable but also more expensive, typically deployed in the cloud. In this setting, a router is used to determine whether the small model is sufficient for a given query 𝐱\mathbf{x} or whether the query should be escalated to the large model. Routing can therefore be naturally formulated as correctness prediction for the small model: if the small model is expected to answer correctly, the system uses its output; otherwise, the query is deferred to the large model.

Formally, let hs​(𝐱)h_{s}(\mathbf{x}) denote the prediction of the small model and hl​(𝐱)h_{l}(\mathbf{x}) denote the prediction of the large one. The router r⁡(𝐱)r(\mathbf{x}) makes a binary decision:

r⁡(𝐱)={0,defer to ​hl​(𝐱),1,use ​hs​(𝐱).r(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{defer to }h_{l}(\mathbf{x}),\\ 1,&\text{use }h_{s}(\mathbf{x}).\end{cases}

Let Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\} denote whether the output of the small model is correct with respect to the ground truth, where Y=1Y=1 indicates correctness. The goal is to design r⁡(𝐱)r(\mathbf{x}) to accurately predict YY, thereby using the small model when it is likely to be correct and deferring to the large model otherwise.

3.2 Probes Trained on Hidden States.

A representative model-aware routing approach uses hidden states of the small model to predict whether its output hs​(𝐱)h_{s}(\mathbf{x}) will be correct. Previous works have demonstrated that hidden states provide a strong signal of the LLM’s confidence, thereby achieving strong performance in text-only LLM routing (Chuang et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2024; Mahaut et al., 2024).

Formally, let θ\theta denote the parameters of the LLM. Given an input query 𝐱=(x1,…,xn)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) with sequence length nn, the model produces a sequence of hidden states at layer ll:

𝐙(l)={𝐳1(l),𝐳2(l),…,𝐳n(l)}∈ℝn×d,\mathbf{Z}^{(l)}=\{\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{1},\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{n}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d},

where dd denotes the hidden dimension. Following previous work (Chuang et al., 2025; Mahaut et al., 2024), the last-token hidden state 𝐳n(l)\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{n} is used as the input of the probe.

A probe gϕ:ℝd→[0,1]g_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow[0,1], parameterized by ϕ\phi, is trained to predict the correctness label YY. The prediction is defined as

y^=σ⁡(gϕ​(𝐳n(l))),\hat{y}=\sigma\big(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{n})\big),

where σ\sigma denotes the logistic sigmoid function. The probe is trained with the binary cross-entropy loss:

ℒprobe​(ϕ)=𝔼x,y​[−y​log⁡y^−(1−y)​log⁡(1−y^)].\mathcal{L}_{\text{probe}}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\big[-y\log\hat{y}-(1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\big]. (1)

The probe learns a mapping from intermediate hidden states to the correctness label YY and therefore serves as a routing estimator. Compared with sequence-level signals such as input difficulty or output consistency, probes can capture richer semantic information encoded in hidden states (Chuang et al., 2025), which leads to effective routing performance.

3.3 Probes Failed in MLLMs.

Although hidden-state probes are effective in text-only LLM routing, their performance degrades substantially in MLLMs. To examine this effect, we conduct two groups of experiments.

First, we use ScienceQA (Saikh et al., 2022), which naturally contains two subsets: a text-only subset and a subset with images. We train and evaluate probes separately on these two subsets. The results show that probe performance, measured by AUC, is consistently lower when images are present. Second, to reduce potential bias caused by differences in the underlying samples, we conduct an additional comparison on A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022) and MMMU (Yue et al., 2024), both of which originally contain only image-text paired samples. For each dataset, we construct a text-only version by prompting GPT to generate descriptions of the images. We then train and evaluate probes on both the original multimodal version and the caption-based text-only version. The results again show that probes perform better on the text-only versions, indicating that the presence of images weakens correctness signals in hidden states and leads to lower routing accuracy.

4 Method

4.1 Aggregation Hidden States for Probing

The empirical results in Sec. 3.3 show that the last token hidden state 𝐳n(l)\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{n}, which is the standard input to probes, provides a weak routing signal in MLLMs. One possible reason is that information relevant to answer correctness is not concentrated in the final token alone. Instead, such information can be distributed across multiple token representations, especially when textual and visual information are jointly encoded.

To address this issue, we construct the probe feature from token-level hidden states in the preceding layer. Let 𝐙(l−1)={𝐳i(l−1)}i=1n\mathbf{Z}^{(l-1)}=\{\mathbf{z}^{(l-1)}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} denote the hidden states at layer l−1l-1. In a transformer, the last token hidden state at layer ll is produced by aggregating information from all tokens’ hidden states in layer l−1l-1 through the attention module. However, this aggregation is optimized for answer generation by the MLLM, rather than for routing. As a result, the resulting representation may emphasize information useful for producing the next token while weakening signals that are more informative for predicting answer correctness. In MLLMs, this issue can be more severe because irrelevant or redundant visual content may also be mixed into the final-token representation. We therefore propose to replace this implicit aggregation with a learned aggregation tailored to routing.

Attention Probe. We define the probe input as

𝐳^=∑i=1nβi​𝐳i(l−1),\hat{\mathbf{z}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{i}\mathbf{z}^{(l-1)}_{i},

where βi\beta_{i} denotes the contribution weight of token ii. The weights are computed with a lightweight attention mechanism:

si=𝐪⊤​𝐳i(l−1)d,βi=exp⁡(si)∑j=1nexp⁡(sj),s_{i}=\frac{\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{z}^{(l-1)}_{i}}{\sqrt{d}},\quad\beta_{i}=\frac{\exp(s_{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(s_{j})},

where 𝐪∈ℝd\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a learnable routing query vector and dd is the hidden dimension. The aggregated representation 𝐳^\hat{\mathbf{z}} is then used as the input to the probe for routing.

This design does not modify the backbone MLLM and only changes how the probe reads intermediate representations. In this way, the probe can focus on routing-relevant cues while reducing the influence of irrelevant visual information that may be carried into the hidden state 𝐳n(l)\mathbf{z}^{(l)}_{n}.

The results in Table 2 show that the Attention Probe consistently improves routing AUC over the standard last token probe across most datasets and backbone models. These results suggest that correctness-related signals in MLLMs are not well captured by the final-token representation alone, and that a learned token-level aggregation provides a stronger feature for routing.

4.2 ReLope

The Attention Probe reweights existing features but does not alter the representation space itself. We next consider a more expressive approach that directly adapts the hidden state for routing. To this end, we introduce ReLope (KL-Regularized LoRA Probe), which combines LoRA adaptation with a variational bottleneck objective. The LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to reshape the hidden representation without full fine-tuning, while the bottleneck encourages the adapted feature to retain information related to answer correctness and discard irrelevant variation.

Model Structure. We insert LoRA adapters into the selected transformer layer ll and keep the original backbone parameters frozen. The LoRA adapters take the hidden states 𝐙(l−1)∈ℝn×d\mathbf{Z}^{(l-1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} at transformer layer l−1l-1 to produce adapted hidden states 𝐙~(l)\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}^{(l)}, from which we can get the last-token representation

𝐳=𝐳~n(l)\mathbf{z}=\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{(l)}_{n}

as the routing feature. Instead of sending 𝐳\mathbf{z} directly to the probe classifier, we first map it to a stochastic bottleneck. Two linear projection heads produce the parameters of a diagonal Gaussian:

𝝁=𝐖μ​𝐳+𝐛μ,log⁡𝝈2=𝐖log⁡σ2​𝐳+𝐛log⁡σ2.\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{W}_{\mu}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b}_{\mu},\quad\log\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}=\mathbf{W}_{\log\sigma^{2}}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b}_{\log\sigma^{2}}.

These parameters define a variational posterior

qψ​(𝐳′∣𝐳)=𝒩⁡(𝝁,diag⁡(𝝈2)),q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{z})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2})),

from which the compressed representation is sampled using the reparameterization trick:

𝐳′=𝝁+𝝈⊙ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈).\mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\sigma}\odot\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\quad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).

The probe prediction is then computed from the compressed feature:

y^=σ⁡(gϕ​(𝐳′)).\hat{y}=\sigma(g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})).

At inference time, we use the posterior mean 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} in place of sampling.

Training Objective. ReLope jointly optimizes probe prediction and representation compression:

ℒ=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}= 𝔼(𝐱,y)​[−y​log⁡y^−(1−y)​log⁡(1−y^)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},y)}\big[-y\log\hat{y}-(1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\big] (2)
+βDKL(𝒩(𝝁,diag(𝝈2))∥𝒩(𝟎,𝐈)).\displaystyle+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}))\;\|\;\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\right).

The first term is the binary cross-entropy loss for routing prediction. The second term regularizes the bottleneck representation by encouraging the posterior to stay close to a standard Gaussian prior. Following the information bottleneck view (Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015; Alemi et al., 2016), this regularization encourages the representation to preserve information that is useful for predicting correctness while discarding irrelevant details in the hidden states. The coefficient β\beta controls the strength of the compression.

Unlike existing routing methods, which make routing decisions from fixed model inputs or outputs, ReLope learns routing-oriented features by adapting the hidden states themselves. This design allows ReLope to make decisions based on features that are more informative for the answer’s correctness in MLLMs and more robust to irrelevant multimodal variation.

5 Experiment

5.1 Datasets

We evaluate ReLope routing performance on five widely used multimodal reasoning benchmarks. MMMU Yue et al. (2024) is designed to evaluate advanced multimodal reasoning across multiple academic disciplines and contains thousands of expert-level questions spanning more than 30 subjects. AOKVQA Schwenk et al. (2022) contains over 25,000 questions and requires both external world knowledge and image understanding ability to answer correctly. ScienceQA Saikh et al. (2022) is a multimodal science question answering benchmark consisting of over 21,000 middle school science problems. ChartQA Masry et al. (2022) is a benchmark for question answering over charts and tables, requiring models to interpret structured visual data and perform logical reasoning with it. MathVision Wang et al. (2024) contains visually grounded mathematics problems, requiring models to interpret diagrams and symbolic expressions in order to solve complex mathematical questions.

5.2 Baselines

We compare ReLope with several representative routing strategies. MoT Yue et al. (2023) performs routing based on multiple reasoning traces generated by the model. The final routing decision is obtained by aggregating signals from different reasoning paths, which provides a more stable estimate of task difficulty. Cascade Routing Chen et al. (2023) adopts a staged routing framework in which inputs are first processed by a lightweight model and are escalated to stronger models only when necessary. We implement Strategy 3 from the original paper, which determines routing decisions based on model confidence signals. RouteLLM Ong et al. (2024) learns a routing function that ranks candidate models according to expected performance and cost. Following the original work, we use the SW Ranking strategy to estimate routing preferences between models. Post-Hoc Embed Gupta et al. (2024) extracts the output embedding of the small model after generation. A lightweight classifier is trained on these embeddings to estimate whether the small model can correctly solve the input problem. Probe Chuang et al. (2025) trains a supervised probe on intermediate hidden states of the model to estimate correctness probability, which serves as the routing signal.

5.3 Implementation Details

All experiments are implemented in PyTorch using the transformers and peft libraries. For probe-based methods (Probe, Post-Hoc Embed, Attention Probe, and ReLope), a five-layer MLP probe is used. Training uses the AdamW optimizer with learning rate 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}. Hidden states are extracted from an intermediate transformer layer ll of the small model fθf_{\theta}. Layer l=24l=24 is used for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct (32 layers), and layer l=40l=40 for Gemma3-12B (48 layers). For ReLope, a LoRA adapter with rank r=128r=128 and scaling factor α=256\alpha=256 is inserted into the selected transformer layer. Two linear heads predict 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} and log⁡𝝈2\log\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2} from the adapted feature 𝐳\mathbf{z}. The loss combines binary cross-entropy and KL divergence with β=1.0\beta=1.0. All experiments run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB memory.

5.4 Comparison with Baselines

AUC performance comparison. Table 2 reports routing performance on five datasets and three backbone MLLMs: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), Gemma3-12B (Team et al., 2025), and Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct (Abouelenin et al., 2025). The Attention Probe and ReLope consistently achieve the best results across all datasets and backbone models. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, ReLope achieves an average AUC of 88.9788.97, improving over Attention Probe by 4.134.13. Similar improvements appear on Gemma3-12B and Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct, where the average AUC achieves 84.8884.88 and 85.9385.93, respectively. These results indicate that hidden state reconstruction improves the routing performance.

Routing performance in the hybrid MLLM system. Following Chuang et al. (2025), we evaluate the trade-off between accuracy and cost in a hybrid MLLM system composed of Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and a stronger large model. We use GPT-4.1 for most datasets and GPT-5.1 OpenAI (2026) for MathVision. Given a routing ratio of h%h\%, each method ranks queries by its routing score and sends the top-h%h\% hardest queries to the large model, while the remaining queries are answered by the small model.

Figure 2 reports overall system accuracy as the routing ratio varies. When the ratio is 0, all queries are handled by the small model; when it is 100, all queries are routed to the large model. ReLope consistently traces the strongest tradeoff across all datasets. Its advantage is most evident at low routing ratios, where it gains higher accuracy under the same budget. This shows that ReLope is better at identifying queries that truly require escalation, leading to more efficient hybrid MLLM routing.

5.5 Ablations and Discussion

Robustness to visual perturbations. To further examine whether ReLope suppresses task-irrelevant visual noise, we evaluate routing robustness under image perturbations. For each test sample in AOKVQA, we apply several typical perturbations to the input image, including Gaussian noise, JPEG compression, and Gaussian blur. The text prompt and ground-truth label remain unchanged. To summarize robustness across perturbation types, we compute the average AUC drop relative to clean inputs: Δ​AUC=AUCc​l​e​a​n−1K​∑k=1KAUCp​e​r​t​u​r​b(k),\Delta\text{AUC}=\text{AUC}_{clean}-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\text{AUC}_{perturb}^{(k)}, where KK denotes the number of perturbation types. A smaller Δ\DeltaAUC indicates stronger robustness.

Table 3 shows that ReLope consistently exhibits the strongest robustness across perturbations. While all routing methods experience performance degradation when visual noise is introduced, the drop is substantially smaller for ReLope. The result suggests that the LoRA adaptation with KL regularization encourages the router to learn representations related to routing filter out task-irrelevant visual noise. As a result, ReLope produces more stable routing decisions.

Generalization on OOD data. We evaluate routing generalization under domain shift. For each target dataset, the probe is trained on the remaining four datasets and evaluated on the chosen dataset. Table 4 shows that ReLope achieves the best performance on four out of five benchmarks, consistently outperforming existing probe-based methods, which indicates stronger cross-dataset generalization. However, the gain on MathVision is smaller. This is expected because MathVision focuses on mathematical reasoning, which differs substantially from the general QA tasks represented by the other datasets. The resulting domain gap makes transferring routing signals learned from general QA datasets more challenging. Nevertheless, ReLope still achieves the best performance among probe-based methods on MathVision, suggesting that the learned routing-aware representations remain more robust under substantial domain shift.

Parameter ablation. Figure 3 shows the impact of three key parameters: the LoRA rank rr, the probe layer ll, and the VIB coefficient β\beta. Increasing the LoRA rank improves routing AUC up to r=128r=128, while further increases provide only marginal gains. This suggests that a moderate rank is sufficient to adapt the hidden representation for routing. For probe placement, intermediate and later transformer layers provide stronger routing signals than early layers, indicating that these layers contain more informative features for correctness prediction. For the VIB coefficient, moderate values (β∈[0.5,1.0]\beta\in[0.5,1.0]) achieve the best performance, suggesting a suitable balance between information compression and predictive accuracy.

6 Conclusion

This work studies routing in MLLMs and shows that probe-based methods, which are effective in text-only LLMs, degrade substantially in the multimodal setting. To address this issue, two methods are proposed. The Attention Probe aggregates token-level hidden states to enrich the probe input, while ReLope introduces a LoRA adapter with a KL regularizer to learn routing-aware representations. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and backbones show consistent improvements over strong baselines. In hybrid systems, our proposed methods achieve a better accuracy–cost trade-off, especially under low routing budgets. These results highlight the importance of learning a routing-aware probe in MLLMs. More broadly, the findings suggest that improving the structure of hidden states is a promising direction for reliable routing in multimodal systems.

7 Limitations

This work has several limitations. First, although the experiments cover multiple benchmarks and backbone MLLMs, the evaluation is still limited to a small set of tasks and model families. It remains unclear how well the proposed methods generalize to other multimodal settings and broader deployment scenarios. Second, ReLope relies on supervised correctness labels and introduces additional tuning overhead, which may limit scalability in new domains. Finally, while we show that standard hidden-state probes are much less effective in MLLMs than in text-only LLMs, the underlying reason is still not fully understood. Our results suggest that multimodal hidden states contain weaker routing signals, but a deeper analysis of why probe methods fail in MLLMs remains necessary.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
